New Jersey property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Any owner may appeal an assessment to the County Board of Taxation; for assessments over $1,000,000 the owner may instead file directly with the Tax Court of New Jersey. (NJ Division of Taxation - Assessment and Appeals; source)
  • Petitions to the county board or Tax Court must be filed and received on or before April 1; where a municipal revaluation or reassessment occurred, the deadline is May 1. (NJ Division of Taxation - Assessment and Appeals; source)
  • Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth Counties use an alternative assessment calendar with a January 15 appeal deadline. (NJ Division of Taxation - Assessment and Appeals; source)
  • To be excessive or discriminatory, an assessment must be shown not to fairly represent the True Market Value Standard or the Common Level Range Standard; the common level range is plus or minus 15% of the district's average ratio. (NJ Division of Taxation - Assessment and Appeals; source)
  • Appeal is made by filing Form A-1 and Form A-1 Comp. Sale with the County Board of Taxation. (NJ Division of Taxation - Assessment and Appeals; source)
  • From a county board judgment, an appeal to the Tax Court must be filed within 45 days of the judgment date. (NJ Division of Taxation - Assessment and Appeals; source)
  • The Director's Ratio (Average Ratio Assessed to True Value) is published in the Table of Equalized Valuations certified on or before October 1 each year. (NJ Division of Taxation - Realty Transfer Fees FAQ; source)
  • All 566 municipalities must hold at least one tax sale per year if there are delinquent taxes or municipal charges. (Elements of Tax Sales in New Jersey | NJ DCA Division of Local Government Services; source)
  • Winning bidder is the one bidding the lowest percentage of interest (bid down from up to 18%) or, at 0-1%, the highest premium. (Elements of Tax Sales in New Jersey | NJ DCA Division of Local Government Services; source)

New Jersey charges a tax or fee on real estate transfers, as described below. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • The State imposes a Realty Transfer Fee (RTF) on the seller for recording a deed, calculated on the consideration recited in the deed. (NJ Division of Taxation - Property Sale Realty Transfer Fee; source)
  • RTF rates for total consideration not over $350,000: $2.00 per $500 up to $150,000; $3.35 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000; $3.90 per $500 from $200,000 to $350,000. (NJ Division of Taxation - Property Sale Realty Transfer Fee; source)
  • RTF rates for total consideration over $350,000: $2.90 per $500 to $150,000; $4.25 to $200,000; $4.80 to $550,000; $5.30 to $850,000; $5.80 to $1,000,000; $6.05 above $1,000,000. (NJ Division of Taxation - Property Sale Realty Transfer Fee; source)
  • Graduated Percent Fee ('mansion tax') on consideration over $1,000,000 for Class 2 residential and certain other classes: 1% over $1M to $2M, 2% over $2M to $2.5M, 2.5% to $3M, 3% to $3.5M, 3.5% above $3.5M; the RTF page says the seller is statutorily responsible for the RTF and this fee. (NJ Division of Taxation - Property Sale Realty Transfer Fee; source)
  • RTF exemptions include deeds between husband and wife or parent and child, deeds for consideration under $100, sales for delinquent taxes, partition, deeds by an executor/administrator to a devisee or heir, and deeds recorded within 90 days after a divorce decree. (NJ Division of Taxation - Property Sale Realty Transfer Fee; source)
  • Partial exemption rates apply to qualifying senior citizens (age 62 or older), blind or disabled sellers, and low/moderate income housing, claimed on Form RTF-1. (NJ Division of Taxation - Realty Transfer Fees FAQ; source)
  • The senior/blind/disabled partial exemption is personal: it cannot be given to a decedent's estate or to a trust. (NJ Division of Taxation - Realty Transfer Fees FAQ; source)
  • Example from DOR FAQ: consideration of $325,000 with no exemption gives an RTF of $1,910. (NJ Division of Taxation - Realty Transfer Fees FAQ; source)

  • Landlord must apply for the warrant within 30 days of the judgment, and have it executed within 30 days of issuance, unless stayed. (Landlord/Tenant | NJ Courts; source)
  • For nonpayment, a residential tenant who pays all rent due plus costs before or on the hearing date, or within three business days after eviction, has the case dismissed. (Landlord/Tenant | NJ Courts; source)
  • Legitimate residential tenants may be protected by New Jersey's Anti-Eviction statute, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12, including when the property is in foreclosure. (Foreclosure Self-Help | NJ Courts; source)
